nameStory: This little acrobat is named after Nicholas Marcellus Hentz, a French-American naturalist who became one of America's first spider experts in the 1800s. The 'palmarum' part comes from Latin meaning 'of the palms,' hinting at this spider's love for plants and sunny spots where it can hunt.
description: The Common Hentz Jumping Spider is a small, athletic hunter that's like the cat of the spider world. These tiny acrobats are usually about the size of a pencil eraser, with compact, sturdy bodies built for precision leaping. They have the characteristic large front eyes of jumping spiders that give them an almost curious, intelligent expression. Unlike web-building spiders, these active hunters stalk their prey during the day.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a square pattern, with the two center eyes noticeably bigger and giving an almost metallic green or bronze shine in good light

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and stocky build like a tiny bulldog, with relatively short, thick legs that feel sturdy rather than delicate if gently touched

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Usually brownish or grayish with lighter stripes or patches, often with a subtle iridescent quality that shifts in the sunlight

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with sudden stops, often turning to face you directly when approached, and may leap several times its body length when startled

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to sit comfortably on a dime, typically 3-5mm in body length not counting legs

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No hunting web, but creates small silk retreats under bark or in plant crevices that feel like tiny silk sleeping bags

habitat: Look for these spiders on tree bark, fence posts, and the sunny sides of buildings where they hunt for small insects. They're particularly fond of rough-textured surfaces like weathered wood or stone walls that provide good grip for their acrobatic hunting style. You'll often spot them in gardens, parks, and wooded edges where there's plenty of insect activity.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter retreats and become active hunters, often seen sunning themselves on warm bark and wooden surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when you'll see the most dramatic hunting displays and courtship dances. Males perform elaborate leg-waving rituals.
seasonality.fall: Mating season continues and females create silk egg sacs in protected crevices. Adults prepare winter retreats under loose bark.
seasonality.winter: Hidden in silk-lined retreats under bark or in building crevices, occasionally emerging on unusually warm days.

funFact: These spiders can see you watching them and will actually turn to track your movements with their big front eyes, sometimes even approaching closer to get a better look at you – they're one of the few spiders that might investigate YOU as much as you're investigating them!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small jumping spiders, but the Common Hentz has that distinctive direct stare and tends to be found on vertical surfaces more than other jumpers. Remember: if it's watching you watch it, it's probably a jumping spider.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Common Hentz,' these spiders are actually part of the 'long-jawed' jumping spider group, though their jaws aren't noticeably longer to casual observers. The name refers to subtle anatomical differences that scientists use for classification.
compareHints: Compared to its relative the White-jawed Jumping Spider, the Common Hentz tends to be more brownish rather than having obvious white markings around the mouth area. It's also more likely to be found on tree bark and wooden surfaces, while other Hentzia species may prefer different microhabitats like low vegetation or rocks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Hentzia relatives, the white-jawed jumping spider is distinguished primarily by its namesake white jaw coloration, which is much more pronounced than in the Common Hentz jumping spider.
Hentzia grenada differs from its relatives the White-jawed Jumping Spider and Common Hentz Jumping Spider primarily in its extremely limited New England range and specific habitat preferences.
